processing: A cultivar made mostly into steamed sencha, and also into pan-fired kamairicha and oolong, where its floral scent gets more room.
harvest_season: Slightly early, about two to three days ahead of Yabukita; the spring first flush is the usual choice.
appearance_dry: As sencha, deep green needles with a floral, sweet smell even before brewing.
appearance_liquor: Clear yellow-green when made as sencha.
appearance_wet: Green leaf typical of sencha, with the floral scent still strong.
taste_profile: A strong floral scent often compared with jasmine, over a solid body with notable astringency and bitterness.

brewing.notes: Sencha settings. This cultivar has real astringency, so stay cool and do not over-steep the first infusion.

vintage_note: Sold in small lots as a single-cultivar spring tea of the current year, mostly as sencha and sometimes kamairicha or oolong. Its scent is the point and it fades, so drink it within the year.
description:
Fujikaori is a Japanese cultivar from Fujieda in Shizuoka, and its name means wisteria aroma. It is one of the most perfumed cultivars you will meet, with a jasmine-like scent that surprises anyone used to ordinary sencha.

That scent is inherited from its Shizuinzatsu 131 parent and comes down to a high level of methyl anthranilate. It is the same compound that gives some grapes their candied smell, which is why one kamairicha made from it has been compared with Concord grape.

The body has more bite than the nose suggests, with noticeable astringency and bitterness. Brew it at about 70 °C and keep the first steep under a minute.

It grows mainly around Fujieda, but small lots come from elsewhere; a kamairicha from Ureshino in Saga is one example. Compare a sencha and a pan-fired version if you can, since the processing changes how the perfume comes across.
history:
Fujikaori was selected from seedlings of a cross between Shizuinzatsu 131 and Yabukita by Ichiji Morizono and Miyoshi Koyanagi of Fujieda City. It was registered in 1996 under Japan's Seed and Seedling Law.

It has stayed a modest local cultivar, spread mainly in and around Fujieda. Growers have to watch for its weaknesses, including frost damage and bacterial shoot blight.
sources_note: Chinese name is a descriptive rendering from 藤かおり.
